content: Preterm birth (PTB) is defined as childbirth occurring before 37 weeks of gestation. It affects approximately 10% of all pregnancies and is a leading cause of neonatal and infant mortality and morbidity, accounting for over half of these adverse outcomes. One of the common causes of PTB is cervical insufficiency, a condition where the cervix is unable to maintain its structural integrity during pregnancy. To address this, one potential intervention is the use of a cervical pessary, a device designed to provide mechanical support to the cervix. However, studies comparing the use of cervical pessaries to other management strategies have yielded inconsistent results, necessitating a systematic review of the available evidence. The objective of this review was to assess the benefits and potential harms of using a cervical pessary to prevent PTB in women with singleton pregnancies who are at risk of cervical insufficiency. Comparisons were made between cervical pessary use and no treatment, vaginal progesterone, cervical cerclage, or bed rest. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted in multiple databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth’s Trials Register, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, up to September 22, 2021. Additional records were identified by reviewing the reference lists of included studies. Only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included, while quasi-randomized trials were excluded. The primary outcome of interest was delivery before 34 weeks of gestation, with secondary outcomes including delivery before 37 weeks, maternal mortality, maternal infection or inflammation, preterm prelabor rupture of membranes, harm to the mother or offspring from the intervention, maternal medication use, discontinuation of the intervention, maternal satisfaction, neonatal or pediatric care unit admission, fetal or infant mortality, neonatal sepsis, gestational age at birth, birthweight, early and late neurodevelopmental morbidity, gastrointestinal morbidity, and respiratory morbidity. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility and risk of bias of the included trials, evaluated the trustworthiness of the data, extracted relevant information, and assessed the certainty of the evidence using the GRADE approach. Eight RCTs involving 2,983 participants were included in the review. Five RCTs (1,830 women) compared cervical pessary with no treatment, three RCTs (1,126 women) compared cervical pessary with vaginal progesterone, and one small study (13 participants) compared cervical pessary with cervical cerclage. When comparing cervical pessary to no treatment, the intervention may reduce the risk of delivery before 34 weeks (risk ratio [RR] 0.72, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.33 to 1.55; low-certainty evidence) or before 37 weeks (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.05; low-certainty evidence). However, these findings are uncertain as the 95% CIs include the possibility of no effect. Cervical pessary likely has little to no effect on the risk of maternal infection or inflammation (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.26; moderate-certainty evidence). The effect of cervical pessary on neonatal or pediatric care unit admission (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.59; low-certainty evidence) and fetal or neonatal mortality (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.48; low-certainty evidence) remains unclear due to wide CIs that encompass both potential benefit and harm. When comparing cervical pessary to vaginal progesterone, the intervention may reduce the risk of delivery before 34 weeks (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.52 to 1.02; moderate-certainty evidence) or before 37 weeks (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.09; moderate-certainty evidence). However, the results are uncertain as the 95% CIs cross the line of no effect. Cervical pessary likely has little to no effect on maternal infection or inflammation (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.12; moderate-certainty evidence). The effect of cervical pessary on neonatal or pediatric care unit admission (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.98; low-certainty evidence) and fetal or neonatal mortality (RR 1.97, 95% CI 0.50 to 7.70; low-certainty evidence) is unclear due to wide CIs. Only one small study with 13 participants compared cervical pessary to cervical cerclage, and the results were inconclusive. In conclusion, the use of a cervical pessary in women with singleton pregnancies may reduce the risk of delivery before 34 or 37 weeks when compared to no treatment or vaginal progesterone. However, these findings should be interpreted with caution due to the low certainty of the evidence. There is insufficient evidence to determine the effect of cervical pessary compared to cervical cerclage. Many prespecified outcomes were reported with low-certainty evidence, and several outcomes of interest were not reported at all. Further high-quality RCTs are needed to provide more robust evidence, particularly in comparing cervical pessary with cervical cerclage and bed rest. Future research should also explore different phenotypes of PTB and be conducted in diverse settings to enhance the generalizability of the findings.
